paragraphs: The paper asks how cortical networks might learn which features of incoming sensory information matter for a task. It treats contextual or instructive signals as supervision that guides the compression of sensory inputs. Its normative approach starts with a mathematical learning objective and derives network behavior from that objective.

The authors use a family of reduced-rank regression objectives that includes reduced-rank minimum mean square error and canonical correlation analysis. These objectives provide different ways to learn a lower-dimensional relationship between inputs and supervisory information. From them, the authors derive offline and online optimization algorithms collectively called Bio-RRR.

The online algorithms can be implemented with networks that update connections using biologically plausible local information. Their learning rules resemble cortical plasticity associated with calcium plateau potentials. Within the model, those potentials can be interpreted as backward-propagating error signals. The algorithms perform competitively with existing implementations of the two named objectives, supporting the possibility that local biological learning rules can approximate useful supervised computations.
neurips-2020-a-simple-normative-network-.tldr: Bio-RRR derives competitive supervised learning algorithms whose local neural updates resemble calcium plateau dependent cortical plasticity.

paragraphs: When labeled examples for a main task are scarce, related tasks can provide extra supervision. The difficulty is deciding how much influence each auxiliary task should have. This paper proposes an automatic weighting method intended to reduce the amount of labeled data required for the main task.

The method interprets the weighted likelihoods of auxiliary tasks as a surrogate prior: a mathematical representation of information about the main task supplied by those tasks. It adjusts their weights to reduce divergence between this surrogate and the main task's true prior. This formulation gives task weighting a statistical objective and avoids a costly grid search over possible weight combinations.

Experiments cover settings including semi-supervised learning and multi-label classification. The authors report that the method uses limited main-task labels more effectively than previous task reweighting approaches. They also report substantial improvement over a baseline in few-shot domain adaptation with only a few extra examples. These findings support automatic weighting as a practical way to make auxiliary supervision more useful under data scarcity.
neurips-2020-auxiliary-task-reweighting-.tldr: Automatically weighting auxiliary tasks through a surrogate-prior objective improves learning when labels for the main task are scarce.

paragraphs: Influence maximization chooses a set of starting nodes to spread influence through a network. A classical model assumes that influence relationships operate independently. This paper studies a more cautious objective: choose seeds that maximize expected spread under the least favorable correlation structure allowed by the model.

The diffusion process can adapt adversarially to the selected seeds. Thus, a seed set is judged by its worst-case expected influence, rather than by spread under one independence assumption. The authors show that this quantity can be computed efficiently for a given seed set. Finding the best set remains NP-hard, but the optimization admits a 1 − 1/e approximation guarantee.

The paper also analyzes the structure of the adversary's diffusion choices and contrasts them with established models. Numerical experiments compare adversarial diffusion with the independent cascade model to investigate the possible cost of assuming independence. The contribution combines a robustness objective with computational guarantees, allowing seed selection to explicitly account for unfavorable dependence between influence relationships.
neurips-2020-correlation-robust-influenc.tldr: A robust influence model selects network seeds against worst-case correlations while retaining efficient influence evaluation and an approximation guarantee.

paragraphs: The paper tackles graph optimization problems in which two opposing players make decisions sequentially under budgets. These problems extend single-player combinatorial optimization because a decision must account for later responses by an opponent. The authors formulate the setting as a zero-sum multi-agent reinforcement learning problem and learn a value-based solution method.

The training curriculum progresses from smaller budgets to larger ones. If an agent can estimate values for instances with budgets up to B, it can examine the possible afterstates of a decision at budget B+1. This examination takes polynomial time regardless of whether the current player maximizes or minimizes. The method uses this relationship to build training datasets from heuristically solved instances with increasing budgets.

For the Multilevel Critical Node problem, the authors report solutions close to optimal on graphs with up to 100 nodes. They also report an average 185-fold speedup over the quickest known exact solver. These empirical results show how a budget-based curriculum can produce useful heuristics for a difficult three-level optimization problem.
neurips-2020-curriculum-learning-for-mul.tldr: A curriculum that increases decision budgets learns near-optimal graph-game heuristics and reports substantial speedups over an exact solver.

paragraphs: Learning from incorrect labels requires understanding how clean labels become noisy ones. A transition matrix represents these class-to-class changes and plays a central role in building statistically consistent classifiers. This paper focuses on estimating that matrix accurately, because errors in it can undermine the classifier that relies on it.

Existing approaches depend heavily on estimates of the noisy class posterior, meaning the probabilities of noisy classes given an input. Randomness in label corruption can make those probabilities difficult to estimate accurately. The proposed dual T-estimator introduces an intermediate class and factors the original transition matrix into two matrices. This divides the estimation problem into components described as easier to estimate.

The resulting method avoids directly estimating the noisy class posterior in the original way. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results support its effectiveness at estimating transition matrices, and the authors report improved classification performance. The central idea is that restructuring the estimation problem can reduce the impact of an unreliable intermediate probability estimate on learning from noisy labels.
neurips-2020-dual-t-reducing-estimation-.tldr: Dual T factors label-noise transitions through an intermediate class to improve transition estimates and downstream classification.

paragraphs: This paper studies active learning of sparse linear decision boundaries, where the learner chooses which examples to label. The boundaries pass through the origin and depend on only s of d coordinates. The guarantees assume an isotropic log-concave distribution of unlabeled inputs and label-flip probabilities bounded by a value η below one half.

The main result is a polynomial-time algorithm with label complexity scaling as s divided by (1−2η) to the fourth power, multiplied by polylogarithmic factors in dimension and inverse target error, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed. This improves the dependence on noise compared with earlier efficient algorithms, whose label requirements deteriorated more severely as η approached one half.

The result is described as the first computationally efficient algorithm in this setting with polynomial dependence on 1/(1−2η). Label requirements still grow as labels become less reliable, but the guarantee remains label-efficient for noise bounds arbitrarily close to one half. The authors also derive improved results for full-dimensional active and passive halfspace learning under bounded noise.
neurips-2020-efficient-active-learning-o.tldr: Under stated distribution assumptions, a polynomial-time active learner improves label complexity for sparse linear classifiers even near the highest allowed noise level.

paragraphs: Missing data are especially difficult to analyze when a value's probability of being absent depends on that value itself. Explicitly modeling this missingness mechanism can complicate inference and require strong distributional choices. This paper extends work on recovering information under such missingness without specifying its distribution, using probabilistic principal component analysis.

Probabilistic principal component analysis represents observations through a low-rank model with random effects. The authors consider a more general missingness mechanism than earlier work on a few self-masked variables in linear regression. They prove identifiability of the model parameters and propose methods for estimating loading coefficients and filling in missing entries.

Both procedures use estimates of the means, variances, and covariances of variables with missing values. These estimates are calculated from observed information by exploiting the data's low-rank structure, and the paper discusses their consistency. Experiments on synthetic data, a medical register, and a recommendation dataset illustrate the method's relevance. The result connects structural assumptions about the data to estimation despite value-dependent missingness.
neurips-2020-estimation-and-imputation-i.tldr: A low-rank probabilistic model supports parameter estimation and imputation when missingness depends on unseen values, without specifying the missingness distribution.

paragraphs: Many differentially private algorithms use the exponential mechanism, which requires drawing samples from a distribution proportional to exp(−f). Sampling can be difficult in high dimensions. A sampling heuristic may produce plausible outputs without supplying the mathematical control needed to establish privacy, making the quality of its convergence guarantee consequential.

Langevin dynamics offers fast sampling methods, but convergence under a familiar distance measure does not automatically provide the guarantee most useful for differential privacy. This paper analyzes discretized Langevin methods using Rényi divergence. For smooth, strongly convex functions f, the authors establish rapid convergence and describe their results as the first convergence guarantees in that divergence.

These guarantees yield fast differentially private algorithms for functions satisfying the stated conditions. The techniques also apply to underdamped Langevin dynamics, extending the analysis to another form of the sampling process. The contribution therefore links computationally attractive samplers to a measure of distributional approximation suited to privacy analysis, rather than relying only on evidence that a sampler approaches its target in some other sense.
neurips-2020-faster-differentially-priva.tldr: Rényi-divergence convergence guarantees for Langevin sampling enable fast private algorithms when the target potential is smooth and strongly convex.

paragraphs: Federated optimization coordinates many agents through a central hub while trying to limit communication. This paper identifies a fundamental issue with some previous procedures: the points at which their updates stop changing need not be stationary points of the intended objective. The problem can occur even with convex objectives and deterministic updates.

The authors introduce FedSplit, a family of methods built from operator splitting for distributed convex minimization with additive structure. Splitting provides a way to organize the components of the optimization across agents. The authors prove that the resulting procedures have the correct fixed points, corresponding to optima of the original problem, and characterize convergence rates in different settings.

The theory also establishes robustness to inexact computation of intermediate local quantities. This matters because the distributed procedure can retain guarantees when agents approximate those quantities. Experiments complement the theoretical results and demonstrate practical benefits. Together, the findings address both where federated updates converge and how reliably they can reach that destination under imperfect local computation.
neurips-2020-fedsplit-an-algorithmic-fra.tldr: FedSplit uses operator splitting to give distributed convex optimization correct fixed points and convergence guarantees robust to inexact local computation.

paragraphs: GramGAN generates three-dimensional textures from a two-dimensional example image. Its goal is to produce high-quality texture that can extend indefinitely while remaining conditioned on the example patch. The synthesis network builds texture by combining learned noise frequencies through nonlinear transformations, giving it a learned mechanism for producing spatial variation.

Its training objective combines ideas from style transfer and generative adversarial networks. The synthesis network matches Gram matrices computed from a discriminator's deep features. These matrices summarize relationships among features, so the objective gives the generator a statistical target for matching the exemplar's appearance through a learned feature representation.

The paper also introduces architectural changes and an extrapolation strategy to improve generalization. In particular, both input and conditioning information influence hidden layers through learned scaling and shifting of activations. Quantitative and visual evaluations across diverse exemplars support the design choices and report better results than previous leading methods. A user study also supports the framework's benefits, adding perceptual evidence to the reported evaluations.
neurips-2020-gramgan-deep-3d-texture-syn.tldr: GramGAN learns indefinitely extendable 3D textures from 2D examples by matching discriminator feature statistics and conditioning hidden activations.

paragraphs: Implicit distributional actor-critic, or IDAC, aims to improve the sample efficiency of policy-gradient reinforcement learning. It combines a critic that models a distribution of discounted returns with an actor that uses a flexible policy distribution. The resulting method operates within an off-policy framework for continuous-action problems.

The critic uses two deep generator networks that receive a state-action pair and random noise. Their outputs approximate a return distribution conditioned on that pair, allowing the critic to represent more than an expected return. The actor mixes policy parameters using a reparameterizable distribution that does not require an analytic density function.

This construction makes the actor's marginal policy implicit while still allowing its parameters and entropy to be estimated. It potentially captures complex covariance and skewness in the policy distribution. On representative OpenAI Gym environments, the authors report that IDAC outperforms leading comparison algorithms on most tasks. The findings support combining flexible return and policy distributions, while the reported advantage remains an empirical result across the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2020-implicit-distributional-rei.tldr: IDAC combines an implicit return-distribution critic with a flexible semi-implicit actor and outperforms comparison methods on most evaluated continuous-control tasks.

paragraphs: Many decision systems first predict uncertain quantities and then use them as coefficients in an optimization problem. End-to-end prediction and optimization trains those predictions according to the decisions they produce. This paper investigates how to obtain the learning gradients needed when the decision stage involves linear programming.

A popular treatment of integer linear programs adds a quadratic penalty to their continuous relaxation so that differentiation methods for quadratic programs apply. The authors instead investigate a logarithmic barrier, a component used in interior-point methods for linear programming. They work with the homogeneous self-dual formulation of the linear program and relate the solver's interior-point step direction to the gradients required for learning.

The approach makes the connection between optimization steps and predictive training explicit through this formulation. In empirical experiments, the authors report performance as good as, or better than, the QPTL and SPO approaches. The stated evidence supports an alternative route to training predictions for downstream optimization, with competitive results obtained from the machinery of interior-point solving.
neurips-2020-interior-point-solving-for-.tldr: An interior-point formulation supplies gradients for training predictions through linear optimization and achieves competitive empirical decision performance.

paragraphs: Recording many neurons simultaneously creates a need for models that summarize population activity in understandable ways. Deep generative models can fit complex neural responses, but their hidden representations can be difficult to interpret and identify. This paper introduces pi-VAE to bring additional structure to those latent representations.

The method combines ideas from latent-variable models and traditional neural encoding models. Alongside neural activity, it models the relationship between latent variables and observable task variables, such as sensory or motor states. These additional relationships constrain the model and connect its hidden representation to measurable aspects of the task. The authors adapt ideas from identifiable variational autoencoders for neuroscience applications.

The paper reports qualitative improvements in interpretability and identifiability from incorporating task variables. It validates pi-VAE on synthetic data and applies it to recordings from rat hippocampus and macaque motor cortex. The authors report better data fits and new insights into neural-code structure. The contribution is a way to combine expressive population modeling with task information that helps make the learned representation scientifically interpretable.
neurips-2020-learning-identifiable-and-i.tldr: pi-VAE links latent neural activity to observable task variables, improving interpretability and identifiability while providing better fits in the reported analyses.

paragraphs: A restricted Boltzmann machine has observed variables in one layer and latent variables in another, with connections only between layers. This paper studies learning such a model from generated samples. Its focus is general models, where existing algorithms can have expensive dependence on the maximum number of observed variables connected to a latent variable.

The new algorithm uses a different structural parameter, s. This counts the largest number of latent variables connected to an observed variable's neighborhood in the marginal Markov random field. Its running time is approximately n raised to 2^s+1, suppressing logarithmic factors. Compared with the stated n^d dependence for previous general-model algorithms, this improves running time when s is less than log₂(d−1).

The authors also give a version that learns a model with small prediction error. Its sample complexity does not depend on the smallest potential in the observed-variable Markov random field. This removes a dependence present in existing methods that cannot be controlled through natural properties of the original restricted Boltzmann machine.
neurips-2020-learning-restricted-boltzma.tldr: A learning algorithm improves runtime for general restricted Boltzmann machines under a stated latent-sparsity condition and offers a prediction-focused sample guarantee.

paragraphs: Predicting rewards can require both an expected value and an estimate of uncertainty. This paper proposes Gaussian process regression as a possible neural computation supporting that combination. Gaussian processes provide a Bayesian framework for nonlinear prediction, and the author constructs neural networks intended to implement that framework.

In the proposed network, first-layer tuning curves correspond to evaluations of the Gaussian process kernel. Hippocampal place cells are offered as an example of such neurons. Output neurons separately represent predictive mean and variance, connecting the architecture to observations of distinct reward-related representations in orbitofrontal cortex.

The weights needed for exact Gaussian process regression do not arise from biological plasticity rules in this construction. The author therefore develops approximations that permit local Hebbian and anti-Hebbian synaptic updates. The resulting network approximates the full Gaussian process well relative to popular sparse approximations and achieves comparable predictive performance. These findings support the computational viability of the proposed neural approximation; the claim that the brain implements it remains a proposal.
neurips-2020-neuronal-gaussian-process-r.tldr: A proposed neural implementation approximates Gaussian process predictions and uncertainty using local biologically motivated learning rules.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering a sparse graph using a Gaussian graphical model whose precision matrix must satisfy graph Laplacian constraints. The learning problem combines maximum likelihood estimation with a penalty intended to discourage unnecessary edges. Earlier approaches used an ℓ1 penalty, following its familiar role in promoting sparsity in graphical lasso.

The authors show that this intuition can fail under Laplacian constraints. Their empirical evidence finds that the ℓ1 penalty does not effectively produce sparse solutions. More strikingly, they prove that a sufficiently large regularization parameter leads to a complete graph, where every pair of vertices is connected. Increasing the supposed sparsity pressure can therefore produce the opposite structural outcome in this problem.

To address this issue, the paper proposes maximum likelihood estimation with a nonconvex penalty and establishes the order of its statistical error. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution highlights how structural constraints can change a regularizer's behavior and provides an alternative designed for this graph-learning setting.
neurips-2020-nonconvex-sparse-graph-lear.tldr: Under Laplacian constraints, strong ℓ1 regularization can produce complete graphs; a nonconvex alternative supports effective sparse graph estimation.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns policies from existing datasets, reducing reliance on collecting new experience through interaction. That makes it relevant where data collection raises cost, safety, or ethical concerns. RL Unplugged provides a benchmark suite for evaluating and comparing methods that learn under this offline setting.

The suite spans games, including Atari, and simulated motor-control tasks, including the DM Control Suite. Its domains vary in whether the agent observes the full state, whether actions are continuous or discrete, and whether dynamics are stochastic or deterministic. This variety allows evaluation across several distinct conditions that an offline learning method may face.

The authors provide domain-specific evaluation protocols and analyze supervised learning and offline reinforcement learning methods using them. They also state plans to release the datasets and implementations. The intended benefits are more reproducible comparisons and access to challenging research tasks with limited computation. The paper presents the suite as an evolving resource that can grow through contributions from the authors and the research community.
neurips-2020-rl-unplugged-a-suite-of-ben.tldr: RL Unplugged supplies diverse datasets and evaluation protocols to make offline reinforcement learning comparisons more systematic and reproducible.

paragraphs: Asynchronous Q-learning estimates optimal action values from one sequence of experience generated by a behavior policy. Successive observations are dependent, so understanding its data requirements involves both learning accuracy and the trajectory's exploration behavior. This paper gives a sharper upper bound for estimating every action value within a target error.

With an appropriately chosen constant learning rate, the bound has two terms, ignoring logarithmic factors. The first scales inversely with minimum state-action occupancy, the fifth power of one minus the discount factor, and squared target error. It matches the corresponding term for independent observations sampled from the trajectory's stationary distribution. The second depends on mixing time and describes an initial cost of reaching steady-state sampling behavior.

That initial cost becomes amortized as learning continues, clarifying how dependence affects the overall sample requirement. The authors report an improvement over the previous bound by at least the number of state-action pairs. They also show that variance reduction can improve the dependence on the discount factor, offering an additional route to better sample complexity.
neurips-2020-sample-complexity-of-asynch.tldr: A sharper Q-learning analysis separates ongoing estimation cost from an initial mixing cost and improves the stated sample-complexity bound.

paragraphs: Point-cloud learning often needs annotations that are cumbersome to collect. This paper investigates self-supervised pretraining for few-shot classification and segmentation, where only scarce training examples are available. Its pretraining is restricted to the same support set used for the downstream task, so the method learns additional representations from that limited collection.

The authors introduce two pretraining tasks based on a cover-tree organization of each point cloud. This hierarchy groups subsets of points inside balls of different radii at successive levels. The tasks encode that hierarchical partitioning, providing training signals from the point clouds' own spatial structure. The trained network then supplies point embeddings as inputs to the downstream network.

In the reported evaluations, supervised methods using this pretraining significantly improve the accuracy of leading methods on classification and segmentation. The approach also outperforms previous unsupervised methods in downstream classification. These findings support using geometric organization to extract useful supervision from a small support set, making the available point clouds more informative before training the final task model.
neurips-2020-self-supervised-few-shot-le.tldr: Cover-tree-based self-supervised tasks improve few-shot point-cloud classification and segmentation using only the available support set for pretraining.

paragraphs: Some games can only be explored by playing them, making exhaustive analysis impractical. This paper asks whether a strategy can still carry a guarantee about how much an opponent could exploit it. It introduces certificates for approximate Nash equilibria in extensive-form games that can provide guarantees without exploring the entire game.

A certificate can be verified in time linear in its own size, rather than the size of the game. For zero-sum games, the authors show that an optimal certificate relative to the exploration completed so far can be computed using standard game-solving methods. This allows the choice of exploration strategy to be separated from the process that establishes the equilibrium guarantee.

Small certificates are not always possible: the paper proves that some families of extensive-form games lack them even under favorable structural assumptions. Nevertheless, experiments find very small certificates, sometimes exact ones, in large and even infinite games. The findings establish both a useful route to exploitability guarantees and a clear theoretical boundary on when compact certification can be expected.
neurips-2020-small-nash-equilibrium-cert.tldr: Compact equilibrium certificates can guarantee limited exploitability without full game exploration, although some game families cannot admit small certificates.

paragraphs: The Swapping Autoencoder is designed to edit existing images through a learned representation. The paper addresses the challenge of making generative models useful for controlled manipulation, where a user starts with a particular image and wants to change selected aspects of its appearance.

The model encodes an image into two independent components and trains swapped combinations of those components to produce realistic images. The training encourages them to represent structure and texture. In particular, one component is encouraged to capture patch statistics that co-occur across different image regions. This gives the model a statistical basis for representing texture separately from structural information.

Because the model includes a trained encoder, it can directly obtain latent codes for a new input image. Those codes support texture swapping, local and global edits, and vector arithmetic in the learned representation. Experiments across multiple datasets report better results and substantially greater efficiency than recent generative models. The findings support designing the representation and training objective around the practical operation of editing real input images.
neurips-2020-swapping-autoencoder-for-de.tldr: The Swapping Autoencoder encourages separate structure and texture representations to enable efficient, controllable editing of real images.

paragraphs: A private synthetic-data generator takes independent samples and releases artificial data that preserves answers to a specified class of statistical queries while providing differential privacy. This paper studies the amount of data needed when that query class need not be finite, extending beyond bounds expressed through the number of queries.

The authors show that every privately proper PAC-learnable class admits a private synthetic-data generator, although the generator may be computationally inefficient. Their construction has sample complexity independent of domain size. By replacing a finite-query requirement with private learnability, the result establishes an equivalence between learning and synthetic generation in the setting considered.

The proof introduces sequential synthetic-data generators. A generator proposes synthetic distributions, and a discriminator attempts to distinguish them from the real distribution through a sequential game. The authors characterize the classes admitting such generators as exactly the Littlestone classes. This connects private synthetic-data generation to a class structure associated with online learning, while the possible computational inefficiency separates the existence result from a promise of a practical fast implementation.
neurips-2020-synthetic-data-generators-s.tldr: Private proper PAC learnability implies private synthetic-data generation, potentially inefficiently, through a sequential framework characterized by Littlestone classes.

paragraphs: Finite-state machines process sequences of bits, and stochastic computing represents continuous values through random bit streams. This paper introduces a way to train multilayer networks of connected finite-state machines. The approach extends their use from single-input functions to more complex computations involving multiple inputs.

The authors show that these networks can synthesize functions such as two-dimensional Gabor filters and perform image classification on stochastic streams. The finite-state machines use lookup tables, allowing these computations without multiplication. The paper then develops a related model for temporal tasks, including character-level language modeling, drawing on the machines' ability to process binary sequences.

For temporal training, the model backpropagates gradients only for the current input step while retaining the ability to learn long-term dependencies. The authors report training-memory requirements of 1/l relative to LSTMs, where l is the number of time steps. They also report 33% lower GPU training power consumption than an LSTM of the same size. These findings connect the model's training procedure to reduced memory and power requirements.
neurips-2020-training-linear-finite-stat.tldr: Trainable finite-state-machine networks support multiplication-free stochastic computation and temporal learning with reported memory and power savings over LSTMs.

paragraphs: Multivariate Hawkes processes model streams of events across a network. Inferring connections from those streams requires more than a single estimated graph: researchers also need to quantify uncertainty in the inferred relationships. This paper develops a statistical framework for that purpose using a directed network whose relationships express Granger causality.

The authors construct a non-asymptotic confidence set for the maximum likelihood estimate of the network Hawkes process. Such a guarantee addresses uncertainty at finite sample sizes instead of relying only on behavior as the amount of data grows without bound. The main mathematical tools are concentration inequalities for continuous-time martingales, used to control fluctuations in the event-driven estimation problem.

The method is compared with a previously derived asymptotic confidence interval for Hawkes processes. An application to reconstructing neuronal connectivity demonstrates the strengths of the proposed approach. The contribution combines estimation with an explicit uncertainty statement, making the inferred network more informative than a point estimate alone. The causal interpretation is specifically the Granger-causal one supplied by the model.
neurips-2020-uncertainty-quantification-.tldr: A finite-sample confidence-set method quantifies uncertainty in Hawkes-network estimates of Granger-causal relationships.

paragraphs: UWSOD trains an object detector using image-level labels, which identify object categories without supplying their locations. The framework addresses three difficulties in weak supervision: generating candidate regions, refining inaccurate boxes, and handling objects at different scales. It integrates these functions without external modules or additional supervision.

An anchor-based proposal generator learns objectness scores and location regression from supervision created within UWSOD. A stepwise refinement procedure progressively selects high-confidence proposals as positive examples and improves both box coordinates and detection scores. A multi-rate resampling pyramid aggregates contextual information across scales, providing an internal feature hierarchy for handling size variation.

Experiments on PASCAL VOC and MS COCO show competitive results with leading weakly supervised detectors. A separate upper-bound evaluation supplies class-agnostic ground-truth boxes and finds performance approaching Faster R-CNN. That result supports the framework's capacity under the extra box information used in this evaluation; it does not establish equivalent fully supervised performance from image-level labels alone. The distinction separates demonstrated weak-supervision results from the architecture's tested upper-bound potential.
neurips-2020-uwsod-toward-fully-supervis.tldr: UWSOD integrates proposal generation, box refinement, and multiscale features for competitive detection from image labels, with stronger capacity shown in an upper-bound evaluation.
